summary:
'FireLens' is an interactive geospatial web application designed to bridge the differences between NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire-detection records, making global burning activity easier to explore and understand.

Using data from NASA FIRMS active-fire observations, we developed a spatial and temporal matching pipeline that associates MODIS detections with corresponding VIIRS observations. Our processed dataset contains 811,293 matched MODIS observations spanning October 2025 to July 2026. We organized these measurements using the H3 hierarchical geospatial indexing system and evaluate an experimental cross-sensor Fire Radiative Power (FRP) calibration model.

FireLens brings this analysis to life through an interactive 3D Earth. Users can explore global hotspot patterns, select geographical hexagons, and examine MODIS FRP, matched VIIRS statistics, and calibrated estimates.

By making complex satellite observations accessible through an intuitive visual interface, FireLens demonstrates how cross-sensor analysis can support researchers, environmental agencies, and fire-management teams in understanding patterns of satellite-observed burning activity.
details:
The Problem

Wildfires, agricultural burning, and other significant thermal events affect ecosystems, air quality, biodiversity, and communities worldwide. Understanding where and when burning activity occurs is essential for environmental monitoring and informed decision-making.

NASA's Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) both detect active fire hotspots, but their differing spatial resolutions, detection characteristics, and observation conditions make direct comparisons challenging.

FireLens addresses this problem by connecting observations from both sensors through a common geographical framework and making the resulting information accessible through an interactive visualization.

Our Solution

We developed 'FireLens', a full-stack web application combining satellite-data processing, spatial-temporal matching, experimental statistical calibration, and interactive 3D visualization.

1. MODIS–VIIRS observation matching

We processed MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations obtained through NASA FIRMS. Using geographical proximity and acquisition-time information, corresponding observations were associated with one another.

MODIS acts as the anchor dataset, with matched VIIRS measurements providing additional statistical information. Our cleaned dataset contains 811,293 matched MODIS observations from October 2025 to July 2026.

2. Geospatial harmonization using H3

We integrated Uber's H3 hierarchical geospatial indexing system to organize observations into consistent spatial units.

Fine-grained resolution-7 H3 cells preserve geographical detail, while resolution-3 aggregation supports efficient global visualization. The resulting visualization dataset contains 7,499 H3 cells, allowing large volumes of satellite observations to be represented as interactive geographic regions.

3. Experimental cross-sensor FRP calibration

Fire Radiative Power (FRP) describes the radiative power associated with a satellite-observed fire detection.

We examined relationships between MODIS FRP and matched VIIRS FRP statistics, comparing VIIRS mean and summed measurements.

We then developed a log-linear regression model that estimates MODIS-scale FRP from summed matched VIIRS FRP.

Using a chronological training and testing split, the VIIRS-sum model achieved a test R² of 0.285 and reduced log-scale mean absolute error from 0.828 to 0.693 compared with a constant baseline.

This demonstrated useful predictive information in the matched VIIRS observations while also highlighting important differences and uncertainty between the sensors. The calibration is presented as an experimental estimate rather than a perfect conversion between instruments.

4. Interactive global visualization

FireLens presents satellite-observed burning activity on a full-screen interactive 3D Earth.

Users can rotate and zoom the globe, explore colour-coded H3 activity overlays, and select geographical cells to open a detailed information panel.

The panel presents matched MODIS observation counts, aggregated MODIS FRP, matched VIIRS FRP, VIIRS match contributions, and the experimental MODIS-scale FRP estimate.

The interface also supports H3 cell selection in locations without matched observations, helping users distinguish displayed activity from areas where the selected dataset provides no records.

Technologies Used

  • Data processing and analysis: Python, Pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Parquet, and scikit-learn.
  • Geospatial indexing: H3, GeoJSON, and spatial aggregation algorithms.
  • Backend development: FastAPI and Uvicorn, providing REST endpoints for geographical activity and cell-level statistics.
  • Frontend development: React, JavaScript, Vite, and CSS.
  • Visualization: React Globe GL, Three.js/WebGL, and Recharts.
  • Environmental enrichment: Google Earth Engine and RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017 for biome/ecoregion context.
  • Development and collaboration: Git, GitHub, and Visual Studio Code.

Creativity and Innovation

FireLens combines a hierarchical hexagonal spatial grid with interactive 3D Earth visualization, allowing users to move from a planetary overview to individual geographical cells.

Instead of presenting separate MODIS and VIIRS datasets, the system associates their observations, exposes their measurement differences, and provides a transparent experimental calibration.

We also used multi-resolution spatial aggregation and selective polygon rendering to balance geographical detail with browser performance.

Our central design principle was to make sophisticated geospatial analysis understandable through a simple experience: explore Earth, select a location, and investigate the satellite observations associated with it.

Intended Impact

'FireLens' demonstrates a foundation for improving the accessibility of cross-sensor fire-activity information.

Potential beneficiaries include environmental researchers, conservation organizations, land managers, disaster-monitoring teams, and educators.

With additional historical records, validated calibration methods, and broader sensor coverage, the approach could support future analysis of seasonal burning activity, unusual conditions, and longer-term changes.

Limitations and Future Development

Our current demonstration uses a matched MODIS–VIIRS dataset covering approximately ten months rather than the complete multi-decade satellite record.

Matching VIIRS observations may also contribute repeatedly across MODIS records, and our experimental calibration has substantial unexplained variation. Aggregated FRP values describe measurements across observations and should not be interpreted as the number of individual fires or total radiated energy.

Future work would extend historical coverage, evaluate calibration across geographical regions and ecosystems, and develop a more complete burning-activity calendar with seasonal baselines.

FireLens provides a working demonstration of how complementary satellite observations can be organized, compared, and explored through an accessible geospatial platform.
